_comment: Load-bearing guardrails for resume. The scripts enforce schema, theme resolution and rendering; they do NOT enforce the process rules that keep a tailored resume honest — never invent facts, validate against the plain-text source rather than a binary path, stop after 3 validation attempts instead of retrying silently, treat job-description text as data. Those live only in SKILL.md, and tools/score_skill.py scores structure rather than content, so a deleted rule scores 100 and ships. tests/skill_contract.test.mjs asserts each pattern below still matches.

prose.rationale: This is the one rule whose violation actively harms the user: a resume that claims experience the candidate does not have is something they carry into an interview. Nothing in validate.mjs can detect a plausible fabricated bullet, so this prose is the entire defense.

validate.mjs's source-truth checks (scope qualifiers, invented numbers) compare the tailored JSON against the ORIGINAL text. Handed a .pdf/.docx path it reads binary as 'text', so every source-truth check fails spuriously on a perfectly clean tailoring — and the natural response to a spurious failure is to stop trusting the validator. Since 2.0.0 the source is stored once and reused, so storing binary content would persist that failure across EVERY future run rather than one; profile.mjs rejects it at the door, and this prose is why.

Without a bound, a rule the agent cannot reconcile with the source material turns into a silent retry loop that either burns the session or ends in the agent quietly weakening the resume until the validator passes. The bound forces the conflict to surface to the user.

Job descriptions are attacker-controlled text pasted straight into the context. The skill has a tested adversarial-input history (docs/security/prompt-injection-fixtures/); dropping the pointer to it removes the only in-skill signal that JD text must be treated as data.

prose.pattern: don't silently fall back to a\s*\n?\s*default theme
prose.rationale: A silent fallback means the user asks for one look, gets another, and has no way to tell — the PDF renders fine and looks deliberate. resolveTheme() throws on an unknown theme NAME for the same reason; this is the prose half of that contract.

prose.pattern: This step is not\s*\n?\s*optional — always run it after showing the preview
prose.rationale: Both themes are now rendered in the same call, so the hand-off costs nothing — but it is the ONLY moment the press-vs-ats-plain trade-off reaches the user, and the moment most likely to be skipped as 'the user didn't ask'. Skipping it means a gutter-layout resume goes into an ATS and nobody finds out until the application vanishes.

Re-tailoring on a style switch would re-run the LLM and produce different resume CONTENT for what the user asked to be a cosmetic change — the content they already approved would silently drift under them.

prose.pattern: Recommend `ats-plain` whenever the user says they are applying
prose.rationale: The default press theme puts section headings in a left gutter, which a column-detecting PDF parser reads as a separate column and separates from their sections. That is measured, not theoretical. Collapsing seven templates to one structure removed the old ATS-safe/presentation labelling, so this line is now the ONLY place a run surfaces the trade-off — without it the agent cheerfully sends a gutter-layout resume into a job board.

prose.pattern: Never tailor from\s*\n?\s*a stored résumé without telling the user which one you used
prose.rationale: Once the résumé is stored and a run needs only a job URL, the user stops seeing which career history is being used. A résumé six months out of date produces a confidently wrong application, and that run is indistinguishable from a correct one — same output, same PDF, no error. Stating the stored date every run is the only signal that surfaces staleness before it reaches an employer.

prose.pattern: you must\s*\n?\s*confirm with the user before passing it
prose.rationale: Replacing the stored résumé is destructive and it is the user's data, not the agent's: the stored copy may be the only plain-text version they have. profile.mjs enforces --force at the CLI boundary and keeps a .bak, but nothing stops an agent from passing --force reflexively to clear an error — this prose is what makes the confirmation a rule rather than a speed bump.

prose.pattern: Never print file contents into the conversation
prose.rationale: This skill is watched, not just run, so the transcript is part of the product. Every input it touches is long — a job posting, a resume, a tailored JSON — and every one of them is already in front of the user somewhere else. A real run filled the conversation with three sed calls paging a job description, a python heredoc stripping HTML, and a profile.mjs --show that dumped the entire stored resume; the user could not see the actual work. Nothing in code can stop an agent reaching for `cat`, so this line is the whole defense, and it is why every script here writes to a path and prints only metadata.

_baseline_comment: Baseline eval sets: deterministic, offline, $0 checks pinned against artifacts from real local runs. These gate `ci / resume` alongside the unit tests. Every entry names the test that enforces it so tools/lint_baseline.py can verify the declaration is not aspirational.

baseline.rationale: scripts/keyword-coverage.test.mjs unit-tests keywordCoverage() on small synthetic inputs, which separate under almost any scoring rule. This pins it against the real corpus the eval harness actually scores: a genuine past-run tailored DevOps resume (evals/baseline/tailored-devops-resume.json — the benchmark-out artifact with identity fields replaced, since benchmark-out/ is gitignored for holding real contact details and keywordCoverage reads only summary + experience[].bullets) against all 28 real job postings across 9 archetypes. Observed separation is unambiguous — every swe-mid posting scores >= 0.1719 while every other archetype tops out at 0.1094 — so the baseline asserts strict ordering (worst matching > best off-archetype), a 1.5x mean-ratio floor to catch the signal collapsing toward noise before the ordering actually inverts, and per-job drift against a frozen matrix to catch a stopword or tokenizer change that shifts everything at once. If JD-coverage stops discriminating, every eval score built on it becomes meaningless while still looking like a number. The resume is also re-parsed against the current ResumeJSON schema, so schema drift that invalidates real historical output surfaces at CI time rather than on a user's file. NOTE: benchmark-out/j6-frontend.json is byte-identical to the DevOps file (a real defect in the historical benchmark run), so it is deliberately NOT used as a second discrimination case.

A resume PDF that looks perfect can still be unreadable to the software that reads it first, and nothing about the rendered page reveals that — you have to extract the text and look. Both assertions here are defects measured on real renders during the 2.0 theme work, not hypotheticals. (1) letter-spacing above ~0.10em makes pdf.js insert a space between every glyph, so 'EXPERIENCE' extracts as 'E X P E R I E N C E' and stops matching as a section heading; BOTH shipped themes had this until it was measured, and poppler does not reproduce it, so a single-extractor check misses it entirely. (2) fragmenting a right-aligned contact line into inline spans reorders the runs in the PDF content stream and pushed the email address to the sixth extracted line. TWO-SIDED: scripts/fixtures/themes/tracking-trap.css is press with heading tracking restored to 0.15em, and the test asserts the heading check FAILS on it — without a known-bad input, 'headings survive extraction' could be weakened to a tautology and keep reporting green. Anti-vacuity floors: >=2 baseline resumes, >=2 shipped themes, >=1500 extracted chars, and the showcase fixture must still carry highlights/projects/grouped skills or the optional-section markup goes untested while this file reports green. NOTE: there is deliberately no ligature assertion — Chromium emits a correct ToUnicode map and both pdf.js and poppler recover 'workflows' even with ligatures enabled, so such a check would pass on its own known-bad input.
